blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant rambutan. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

This guide shows how Filipino growers usually plant a grafted rambutan of a good variety and care for it until the first fruits. It is for backyards and small orchards in warm, humid places.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for fruit and plantation trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [rambutan varieties sold here](/crop-varieties/rambutan). If the leaves turn pale later on, the [rambutan nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/rambutan-nutrient-deficiency) helps you find what is missing. For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).
When to plant rambutan
Grafted seedlings are planted as the rains begin, around May to July, so they settle in with steady rain. Rambutan likes a warm, humid place with rain spread through much of the year.
What you plant

A grafted seedling of a proven variety, such as R5, R162, Rongrien or another sweet, red fruited selection, joined to a seedling rootstock. Rootstocks are grown from fresh seed for about 8 to 12 months, grafted, and planted out about 6 months after grafting. Trees from seed take longer to bear and give mixed fruit, and many seedlings turn out to be male trees with few or no fruits.
Paano magtanim ng rambutan, step by step
Rambutan usually starts bearing at about 4 to 5 years. The crop is ready about 5 years after planting.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 30 days before planting: Clear the land and mark the spots
items.text: Clear the brush and stumps and loosen the soil. Mark the planting spots about 8 to 10 m apart each way, since rambutan grows into a wide tree.

items.title: 7 days before planting: Dig the holes
items.text: Dig holes at least 30 cm wide and 30 cm deep, wider than the seedling bag on hard soil. Mix the topsoil with compost or dried manure for filling back.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant the grafted seedling
items.text: Remove the bag without breaking the soil ball and set the seedling in the hole with the graft above the soil. Fill in with topsoil, press it gently and water well.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 1: Shade the new tree
items.text: Shade the new tree with fronds or a net for its first weeks, and longer if the weather is hot and dry, so it recovers from planting. Water it in dry spells and mulch around the base.

items.title: Day 30: First fertilizer
items.text: Put about 60 g, or 6 tablespoons, of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) around the base and cover it lightly with soil. Repeat a few times a year, a little more as the tree grows.

items.title: Month 3: Ring weed every three months
items.text: Weed a circle around each tree every three months or whenever the grass grows back. Lay the cut grass as mulch a little off the stem.

items.title: Month 4: Remove rootstock shoots
items.text: Rub off any shoot that comes from below the graft. Keep the good variety growing as the main stem.

items.title: Month 6: Watch for twig borers and mealybugs
items.text: Look for twigs that wilt or have small holes, and for white mealybugs on new shoots. Cut and burn damaged twigs.

items.title: Month 12: Feed more in the second year
items.text: From the second year, give about 200 g of complete fertilizer a tree, about 300 g in the third year and about 400 g in the fourth. Split each year's amount between the start and the end of the rains.

items.title: Month 18: Shape the young tree
items.text: Keep a few strong, well spread main branches and cut out weak, crossing or low branches. A low, open tree is easier to pick and to protect.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Year 5: First fruits
items.text: Pick when the skin turns pinkish red or fully red, going over the tree in rounds since the fruits ripen unevenly. Cut the bunches with shears or a pole hook without breaking the branches, which bear the next crop.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for rambutan
Spacing
About 8 to 10 m between trees and between rows, one grafted seedling a hole. Holes about 30 cm wide and deep, wider on hard soil.
Water
Mostly rain fed. New trees are shaded and watered in dry spells, and the base is kept mulched. Growers with water on hand irrigate in long dry months so the trees flower and fruit well.
Fertilizer

Compost or dried manure in the hole. About 60 g of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) around a young tree at first, then about 200 g a tree in the second year, 300 g in the third and 400 g in the fourth, split between the start and the end of the rains. Bearing trees get more, with potash for sweet fruit. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

Shading new trees for the first weeks, ring weeding every three months, mulching, removing rootstock shoots, shaping to a low, open tree, and cutting and burning twigs hit by borers. Checking new shoots and fruits for mealybugs and fruit borers.
When and how to harvest

Fruit is ready when the skin turns pinkish red to red, and the fruits in one bunch ripen at different times, so growers pick in rounds, often three times a week at the peak. Bunches are cut with shears or a hooked pole, kept in the shade, sorted by size and ripeness and packed in boxes with air holes.
Common mistakes when planting rambutan

items: Planting seedlings from seed, which may turn out to be male trees with few fruits.
Planting in full sun with no shade in the first weeks.
Tearing branches when picking, which costs the next crop.
Picking whole bunches at once while many fruits are still green.
Leaving twig borer damage on the tree.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of rambutan
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Plant grafted seedlings of a proven variety from an accredited nursery.
Test the soil and feed by the result, raising the amount each year.
Water during long dry spells so flowering and fruit set stay even.
Prune lightly after each harvest to keep the tree low and open.
Scout for twig borers, fruit borers and mealybugs every month and clean up fallen fruit.
Pick in rounds with shears and sort the fruit for a better price.
